1. The Question Nobody Asks
2. Everything Is Numbers
3. Cutting Messages Into Pieces
4. The Roads for Data
5. Finding the Right Machine
6. The Cloud Is a Real Place
7. A Tool, Used Wisely

internet: the huge network linking computers across the world
data: information stored as numbers a computer can use
packet: a small piece that a message is broken into to be sent
cable: a line, often of glass fibre, that carries data
address: the unique number that finds a machine on the internet
data centre: a large building full of computers that stores data

You send a message, and a second later it arrives on a phone across the city. You tap a video, and it plays. This happens so smoothly that almost nobody stops to ask the obvious question. How? How does a message actually travel from your hand to someone else's, through the air and across the world, in the blink of an eye?

image.note: A child tapping send; the message vanishing into a mystery of glowing lines; curiosity

pages.text: The answer is one of the cleverest human inventions of all, and it is not magic. It is the internet, a vast network linking billions of machines together so they can pass messages to one another. Once you understand a few simple ideas, the mystery falls away, and something even more amazing takes its place: understanding.

image.note: A pulled-back view of countless devices worldwide all joined by glowing threads; the whole network

pages.text: Here is the first secret. Inside every computer and phone, everything, every word, every picture, every song, every video, is stored as nothing but numbers. A photograph is really a huge grid of numbers describing each tiny dot of colour. A message is numbers standing for letters. To a computer, the whole world is turned into numbers.

image.note: A photo zooming in until it becomes a grid of numbers; a message shown as its number code

pages.text: Because everything is numbers, it can all be sent as a stream of tiny signals: on or off, on or off, incredibly fast. This simple on-or-off code is the only language computers truly speak, but they speak it billions of times a second. Every marvel on your screen is built from that plainest of alphabets: on, and off.

image.note: A flow of tiny on/off signals streaming down a wire, building into a picture at the end

pages.text: Now, sending a whole large message in one go would be slow and clumsy. So the internet does something clever. It chops your message into many small pieces, called packets, like tearing a long letter into numbered scraps. Each packet is labelled with where it came from, where it is going, and its place in the order.

image.note: A message being cut into small numbered packets, each with an address tag; organised, clever

pages.text: These packets are then sent off separately, and here is the surprise: they need not even travel the same way. Like travellers heading to one wedding by different roads, the packets race across the network by whatever route is quickest, then are put back in order at the far end. The whole message is rebuilt, perfectly, in an instant.

image.note: Numbered packets taking different paths across a network, then reassembling in order at the end

pages.text: What roads do these packets travel? Some of the journey is through the air, as radio signals between your phone and a nearby mast. But most of the internet's great distances are crossed through cables, including vast bundles of glass fibre lying along the bottom of the oceans, carrying light between the continents.

image.note: A world map showing undersea cables linking continents; ships laying cable; the hidden backbone

pages.text: It surprises many people to learn that the internet is a real, physical thing. It is not floating in the sky. It is millions of miles of cable, thousands of masts, and huge buildings full of humming machines, all joined together. When you send a message overseas, it very likely races through a cable lying deep under the sea.

image.note: A giant undersea cable on the ocean floor, light pulsing through it; solid, physical, real

pages.text: With billions of machines connected, how does your message find the one right phone among them all? Every machine on the internet has its own address, a unique string of numbers, rather like every house on an estate having its own number. Your packets carry the address of their destination, and the network delivers them to exactly the right door.

image.note: An estate of houses each with a unique number; a labelled packet being delivered to the right one

pages.text: When you type the name of a website, a special service quietly looks up the numbered address that goes with that name, the way you might look up a friend's number by their name in your contacts. You get to use easy names, while the machines use the numbers. It all happens in a fraction of a second, unseen.

image.note: A website name being matched to its number address in a lookup, like a phone contact list

chapters.title: The Cloud Is a Real Place

pages.text: People speak of saving things "in the cloud", as if photos floated in the sky. But there is no cloud up there. When you save something to the cloud, you are really sending it to a huge building full of computers, called a data centre, somewhere far away, where it is stored safely and can be fetched back whenever you want it.

image.note: A vast data centre, endless rows of humming servers, cooling fans; the real "cloud"

pages.text: These data centres are enormous, use a great deal of electricity, and hold the messages, photos and videos of the whole world. So when your photo appears again on a new phone, it did not come from the sky. It travelled, as numbers, in packets, along cables, from a real building full of real machines, back to your hand.

image.note: A photo travelling from a distant data centre, along cables, back onto a child's new phone

pages.text: The internet is one of the most powerful tools ever built. It puts the knowledge of the whole world within a child's reach and lets friends and families stay close across any distance. Used well, it is a window onto everything humans have ever learned. Few generations before yours have ever held such a thing in their hands.

image.note: A child happily learning and video-calling family on a tablet; the internet at its best

pages.text: But every powerful tool must be handled with care. Not everything on the internet is true or kind, and it is wise to be thoughtful about what you believe, what you share, and how much time you give it. The internet is a marvel, built from numbers, packets and cables. Understand it, respect it, and it will serve you well.

image.note: A child closing a tablet and going outside to play in the sun; balance and wisdom; closing
